ask: The opening blessing. Most Marathi Buddhist families follow Babasaheb Ambedkar's 22 vows, and one of them is not to worship Ganesha. So a Ganesha-only opening speaks for one family. The idea: ॥ श्री गणेशाय नमः ॥ and ॥ नमो बुद्धाय ॥ side by side as equals, with one blessing both can say beneath them: ॥ भवतु सब्ब मङ्गलं ॥, may every blessing be yours. Is that right for both families?

Which rites happen at the Shaadi. Sindoor daan is the heart of a Bihari wedding. Many Buddhist weddings leave out sindoor, the mangalsutra, kanyadaan and the pheras, and use the three refuges, the five precepts and a white thread instead. Which of these happen decides what the Shaadi chapter can say.
Where in Bihar his family comes from: Mithila, Bhojpur or Magadh. That decides which customs and song names we use (matkor, chumavan, kohbar, mangal geet).
Her family's words. Do they want "Namo Buddhaya", "Jai Bhim" or Babasaheb named? Do they keep the haldi? Would they like a Buddha image beside the Ganesha?

bridges.text: Bihar is named after Buddhist monasteries. The word comes from vihāra.
Ajanta, in Maharashtra, paints a king of Mithila. Cave 1 tells the story of King Mahajanaka of Mithila, painted around 470 CE.
An old Pali poem walks from her side to his. Sixteen students set out from the Godavari, through Paithan (home of the Paithani), to Vaishali and Magadha.
Born in Bihar, taken up again in Maharashtra. The Buddha awoke at Bodh Gaya. In 1956 Babasaheb Ambedkar took up the Buddha's path at Nagpur.
One word blesses every wedding: mangal. Bhojpuri mangal geet, the Marathi mangalashtak and the Pali Mangala Sutta.
Women on both sides sang at the grinding stone: jatsar in Bihar, ovi in Maharashtra, where wedding turmeric is still ground to song.

chapters.name: The blessing
chapters.beat: Each family opens with its own invocation, side by side and equal, and one blessing joins them.

his.title: Ganesha, a Mithila (Madhubani) painting
his.note: His Ganesha, painted in Bihar itself. Bright and folk, unlike the court painting on the site now.
zoom: the many hands, each holding something

his.title: Indra worships Ganesha (on the site now)
his.note: The painting you liked. It's beautiful but not from Bihar. Keep it if you prefer.

hers.note: The lotus-bearer of Ajanta Cave 1, the best-loved image of Maharashtra's Buddhist heritage. A gentle figure rather than a god to worship.
zoom: the blue lotus in his hand

hers.note: Devotees climb with trays of white lotuses: an offering scene from Ajanta, in a 1911 copy.

both.note: Her faith, carved in his land: the Buddha's awakening at Bodh Gaya, made in Bihar about 900 years ago.
zoom: the Buddha under the Bodhi tree
the tiny scenes of his life around him
elephants and lions at the base

both.note: If the families prefer no figures at all: the lotus belongs to both, in Buddhism and in Mithila's wedding art.

lines: his
His family opens every good beginning with Ganesha, the remover of obstacles.
hers
Her family opens with the Buddha: Namo tassa, homage to the Awakened One. ⚑
both
Both families bless a wedding with the same old word, mangal: everything good, wished together.

chapters.name: Two homes
chapters.beat: Where each of them comes from, and the threads that already ran between Bihar and Maharashtra long before they met.

his.note: Women raising baskets of fruit from the river. To anyone from Bihar this is Chhath: home in one picture.
his.care: Wellcome's catalogue only says "bathing in the Ganga" and "India". Reading it as Chhath, probably Patna, is ours.

his.note: Patna's main street in 1814, painted by Sita Ram.
The Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya in the 1870s, before it was restored. Where his land and her faith meet.
his.care: It shows the temple overgrown, which may feel melancholy.

hers.note: From a Paithan wedding story of about 1850: two families meet and the two mothers embrace. Painted in the town the Paithani is named after.
hers.care: It is a Hindu epic story, but the scene shows families, not gods. The big figure is the hero Ghatotkacha; keep captions about the mothers.

hers.note: Raja Ravi Varma's Maharashtrian woman: a gold-bordered silk sari, a nath and a tray of fruit.
Pune around 1875: Parvati hill across the lake.
Inside the Karla cave near Lonavala, carved 2,000 years ago: Buddhist Maharashtra, just outside Pune.

both.note: The bridge: Ajanta's wall painting of King Mahajanaka of Mithila. Painted in Maharashtra, set in Bihar, 1,500 years ago.
both.care: In the story the king later leaves his queen. Use the court and the palace, not the plot.

both.note: One map of 1782 with both "Bahar" and "Poonah" on it. The view could travel from one to the other.
both.care: Don't zoom into the corner cartouche (a colonial allegory).

lines: his
His Bihar takes its very name from vihara, the old word for a Buddhist monastery.
hers
In Ajanta, in her Maharashtra, painters told the story of a king of Mithila.
his
The Buddha's awakening came under a peepal tree at Bodh Gaya, in his Bihar.
hers
In 1956 Babasaheb Ambedkar took up the Buddha's path at Nagpur, in her Maharashtra. ⚑
both
An old Pali poem walks sixteen students from the Godavari, through Paithan, all the way to Magadha.

chapters.name: Haldi
chapters.beat: Turmeric, women's songs and blessings. His family's earth and turmeric, her family's ushti halad.

his.note: Women at a Patna market behind baskets of spices and grain, turmeric among them. A warm, colourful Bihari scene.
zoom: the woman weighing on her scales

his.note: A Mithila painting: two women at a rite under a canopy, ringed by pots. The museum doesn't say which rite.
his.care: Only 25 cm wide and simply drawn, so the zooms will be soft.

hers.note: From the same Ajanta story: women bathe the king of Mithila before a great day. The closest ancient picture to a haldi bath.
hers.care: As always at Ajanta, the women are bare above the waist. Ask whether the elders are comfortable.

both.note: The safe choice that belongs to everyone: a botanical plate of turmeric, with flower, leaf and root. The captions carry the customs.
zoom: the root, where haldi comes from

lines: his
Bihar's weddings begin with matkor: women dig sacred earth, singing, to build the wedding hearth. ⚑
hers
In Maharashtra, turmeric touches the groom first; what is left, ushti halad, goes to the bride. ⚑
his
At chumavan, married women bless the couple, touching them with rice, dub grass and turmeric.
hers
In Pune's villages, women still grind the wedding turmeric at the stone mill, singing ovi.
both
Today it is one bowl of turmeric: his blessing first, then carried over to her. ⚑

chapters.name: Sangeet
chapters.beat: Drums, songs that tease, and dancing on both sides.

his.note: A Patna celebration of about 1795: drums, dancing and colour flying in one long room. Full of people to zoom into.
his.care: Very wide with a plain wall above, so the tour stays on the lower half.

his.note: Singers and drummers by Sewak Ram, Patna's best-known painter. Set at a Durga Puja, so it's a festival for one faith.

hers.note: Fugdi, the Marathi women's spinning dance, printed by the Chitrashala Press in Pune around 1890.
hers.care: The crowned figure on the right may be Krishna in costume; caption it simply as fugdi.

hers.note: A Paithan painting of drummers and a long tutari horn with rearing horses: Marathi festival sound.
A tambura from Maharashtra: the gourd is painted with dancers among flowering trees.

chapters.none_both: The famous Ajanta scene of a dancer with musicians (from the Mithila story) would be perfect here, but no large, openly licensed copy exists.
lines: his
After the baraat leaves, Bihar's women stay home and dance domkach, teasing everyone in song.
his
Bihar's gali are cheeky songs that tease the new in-laws; nobody is spared, everyone laughs. ⚑
hers
Expect a fugdi too: Marathi women hold hands and spin, faster and faster, until someone laughs.
both
Women on both sides sang over the grinding stone: jatsar in his Bihar, ovi in her Maharashtra. ⚑

chapters.name: Shaadi
chapters.beat: The procession, the blessing of the elders and the vows. What we say here waits on the families (see the questions at the top).

his.note: The baraat at night: torches, a band, and the groom in a crown in his palanquin under the stars.
his.care: Wellcome says only "India". The style points to Patna; caption it "North India" unless you're happy with "probably Patna".

his.note: A daytime baraat on mica: flags, drums and a long line of musicians.
A pink sari with gold embroidery, made in Patna: a Bihari wedding textile.

hers.note: A Marathi wedding painting from Paithan, about 1850: the bride bows and the elders bless her. Women in nine-yard saris.
hers.care: From a Hindu epic wedding story, but the scene is family and blessing, with no gods.

hers.note: The end of a 19th-century bridal Paithani: parrots, peacocks and flowering trees in silk and gold.
hers.care: LACMA says "probably Paithan". The colours are softer than a modern Paithani.

hers.note: Couples carved arm in arm at the Karla cave near Pune, about 2,000 years ago, on either side of the Buddha.
hers.care: The women are bare above the waist (ancient convention).

both.note: Mango leaves hang as a toran over both families' doors. A 1683 plate for a small detail, not a tour.
both.care: The colourist painted the fruit purple-blue; use the leaves.

lines: his
In Bihar the vow is sealed with sindoor daan, vermilion from his hand in her hair parting. ⚑⚑
hers
Her side begins with candles before the Buddha and Babasaheb, then the three refuges and five precepts. ⚑
hers
A white thread joins them across a pot of water while the Mangala Sutta is chanted. ⚑
his
The Buddha's advice to husbands and wives was given at Rajgir, in his Bihar.
both
Rice from his side, petals from hers: tonight the blessings fall on both of them together.

gaps: Ajanta's dancer-and-musicians scene from the Mithila story: no large, openly licensed copy (the V&A's are non-commercial only).
A painting of a Bihari wedding ceremony itself, a sinhora, Sujani, Manjusha, Tikuli or Bhagalpur silk: nothing openly licensed. Open Mithila art is limited to Cleveland's 11 sheets.
A 19th-century photograph of a Marathi wedding, or a good Lavani image: none found.

Left out on purpose: modern photos of identifiable strangers (a haldi, Deekshabhoomi crowds, a dhol-tasha drummer); Ram and Sita pictures (Ambedkar's vows name Rama, and Sita's marriage is also remembered as sad); Hindu deity prints for her side.
Your own photos would beat all of this for some chapters: her family's Paithani, his family's sinhora, the haldi bowl.
licence: Everything here is CC0 or public domain, except the Ajanta and Karla photographs (CC BY 2.0) and the Kanheri, Deekshabhoomi and Wikimedia photos marked CC BY-SA. Those need the photographer's name in the site's art credits, which the footer already has.

Some old paintings come from Wikimedia Commons copies of British Library and Houston museum works. They rely on the rule that a faithful photo of an old painting is public domain, which US law accepts.
The Ajanta copies are from Lady Herringham's 1915 book (public domain). I skipped one plate made by Nandalal Bose, which is still protected in some countries.
Before anything goes on the site I'll recheck each licence on the museum's own page and record it in docs/05-art-sources.md.
